# Bayes factors for slowdown scenarios ::: {.cell} ::: This chapter calculates Bayes factors [@kass1995bayes] for $e_0$ changes since 2010, assuming different rates of slowdown expressed as a percentage of the average prior (1991–2010) rate of change. The Bayes factor compares the likelihood of the observed post-2010 annual changes in life expectancy under a proposed slowdown scenario against their likelihood under the null scenario of no change from pre-2010 improvement rates: values above 1 indicate support for the slowdown scenario over the no-change scenario. Because the corrected likelihood produces Bayes factors that overflow `exp()` for long observation windows, magnitudes are reported throughout on a $\log_{10}$ scale ($\log_{10}\mathrm{BF} = \log\mathrm{BF} / \log 10$). ::: {.callout-note} ## The corrected likelihood function Earlier drafts of this analysis depended on a likelihood function `get_ll` that contained an operator-precedence error: the term intended as `1 / (2 * sig_sq)` was written `(1 / 2 * sig_sq)`, which R parses as `0.5 * sig_sq`. This attenuated every Bayes factor toward 1 by a factor of $\sigma^4$ (three to four orders of magnitude for annual $e_0$ change), which is why the original manuscript reported Bayes factors indistinguishable from 1 despite years of accumulated evidence. **The bug is fixed here**: this chapter now sources the corrected engine from `R/bayes_factors.R`. The BF-*maximising* slowdown percentage is a monotone transform of the sum of squares and is therefore unaffected by the fix; only the magnitudes change. A full quantification of the fix's impact on the original 2011–2018 findings is given in the audit appendix. ::: This update also extends the actual $e_0$ series to 2024 and, because the 2020–2021 pandemic years are not ordinary draws from the pre-pandemic process, presents three observation-window variants: a **pre-pandemic headline** (2011–2019), the **full series** (2011–2024), and a **COVID-excluded** series (2011–2024 dropping 2020 and 2021). The pre-pandemic window is treated as the headline and its forecast is validated out-of-sample against 2020–2024 below. Now, let's determine the average change (and SD) from 1991 to 2010 — the calibration window, unchanged from the original analysis. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ch_e0_dta %>% filter(between(year, 1991, 2010)) %>% group_by(population, sex) %>% summarise( mean_ch = mean(ch_e0), sd_ch = sd(ch_e0), .groups = "drop" ) %>% write_to_table(here("data", "mean_sd_ch_preslowdown_ons.csv")) %>% mutate(mean_ch = mean_ch * 52.25, sd_ch = sd_ch * 52.25) %>% ggplot(aes(x = mean_ch, y = sd_ch, shape = sex, colour = sex)) + geom_point() + geom_text_repel(aes(label = population, colour = sex), show.legend = FALSE) + labs( x = "Mean annual change in life expectancy in weeks", y = "Standard deviation in annual change in life expectancy in weeks", title = "Mean and standard deviation of change in life expectancy\nfrom 1991 to 2010 by UK population", caption = "Source: ONS Single Year Lifetables" ) ggsave(here("figures", "mean_sd_preslowdown_improvement_ons.png"), height = 20, width = 20, units = "cm", dpi = 300) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](04_bayes_factors_files/figure-html/fig-mean-sd-preslowdown-1.png){#fig-mean-sd-preslowdown width=672} ::: ::: For each of these populations, we can estimate the relative likelihood of observing the observed life expectancies from 2011 onwards under the assumption that each population's fundamentals of life expectancy improvement had not changed after 2010. This assumption is questionable for Northern Ireland because of its changepoint in the mid 1980s, but will be applied to this population too for consistency with the other populations. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Three observation-window variants. Each is calibrated on 1991-2010 and scores # the same 0-100% slowdown scenarios; they differ only in which post-2010 years # are treated as observations. variant_defs <- tibble::tribble( ~variant, ~after_first, ~after_last, ~drop_years, "Pre-2020", 2011L, 2019L, list(integer(0)), "Full series", 2011L, 2024L, list(integer(0)), "COVID-excluded", 2011L, 2024L, list(c(2020L, 2021L)) ) run_variant <- function(dta, after_first, after_last, drop_years) { d <- dta %>% filter(!year %in% drop_years[[1]]) calc_bayes_factors( dta = d, before_period = c(1991, 2010), after_period = c(after_first, after_last), outcome_var = ch_e0 ) } bf_all <- ch_e0_dta %>% select(-e0, -source) %>% group_by(population, sex) %>% nest() %>% crossing(variant_defs) %>% mutate( bayes_df = pmap( list(data, after_first, after_last, drop_years), run_variant ) ) %>% select(population, sex, variant, bayes_df) %>% unnest(cols = c(bayes_df)) %>% ungroup() %>% mutate( population = factor(population, levels = populations), variant = factor(variant, levels = c("Pre-2020", "Full series", "COVID-excluded")) ) # BF-maximising scenario for each population / sex / variant. bf_argmax <- bf_all %>% group_by(population, sex, variant) %>% slice_max(log_bf, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>% ungroup() %>% transmute( population, sex, variant, slowdown_pct = 100 * (1 - perc), log10_bf = log_bf / log(10), mu_best = mu ) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-important} ## Headline: the pre-pandemic (2011–2019) window ::: {.cell} ::: Restricting the observation window to the pre-pandemic 2011–2018 span exactly reproduces the original paper's headline: a 61% slowdown for UK females and 61% for UK males (matching manuscript Table 4), confirming that the corrected engine and the 2024-extended data recover the published result. Extending the pre-pandemic window by the single further year 2019 — a strong recovery year (UK $e_0$ rose 0.29 years for females and 0.24 for males, both above the 1991–2010 mean) — already pulls the pre-pandemic estimate down to a **49% (females) and 56% (males)** slowdown. The pre-pandemic signal is therefore in the ~50–60% range, close to but slightly below the original paper's 61%. ::: The following tables report, for each population and sex, the slowdown percentage $100(1-\text{perc})$ at which the Bayes factor is maximised and the $\log_{10}$ Bayes factor at that maximum, for each of the three observation-window variants. ::: {#tbl-bf-maximise .cell} ```{.r .cell-code} argmax_table <- bf_argmax %>% mutate(cell = paste0(round(slowdown_pct), "% (log10 BF: ", formatC(log10_bf, format = "f", digits = 2), ")")) %>% select(Population = population, Sex = sex, variant, cell) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = variant, values_from = cell) %>% arrange(Population, Sex) argmax_table %>% kable(caption = "BF-maximising slowdown (% below the 1991-2010 mean improvement) and log10 Bayes factor, by observation-window variant.") %>% kable_styling() %>% add_header_above(c(" " = 2, "Observation window" = 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Bayes-factor schedules for the headline (pre-2020) window: log10 BF against # slowdown %, faceted by population and sex. Saved to a NEW suffixed filename so # the committed A12 figure is not overwritten. bf_all %>% filter(variant == "Pre-2020") %>% mutate(slowdown_pct = 100 * (1 - perc)) %>% ggplot(aes(x = slowdown_pct, y = log_bf / log(10))) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") + geom_line() + facet_wrap(population ~ sex, scales = "free_y") + labs( x = "Percentage slowdown from 1991-2010 improvement", y = "log10 Bayes Factor\n(>0 means support for a slowdown)", title = "Bayes Factor schedules for proposed levels of slowdown", subtitle = "Headline pre-pandemic observation window, 2011-2019" ) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, by = 20)) ggsave(here("figures", "A12_Bayes_Factor_Schedules_2024.png"), height = 25, width = 30, units = "cm", dpi = 300) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](04_bayes_factors_files/figure-html/fig-bf-schedules-1.png){#fig-bf-schedules width=1152} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: Read across the variants, the UK as a whole shows a clear three-way tension. The pre-pandemic headline points to a slowdown of roughly 49% (females) and 56% (males), consistent with — and, for the 2011–2018 sub-window, identical to — the original paper's ~61%. The **full series to 2024 inflates this to 65% (females) and 74% (males)**, but that inflation is driven almost entirely by the 2020 shock (UK $e_0$ fell 0.88 years for females and 1.20 for males in 2020), which a Normal-iid likelihood wrongly treats as an ordinary draw. Conversely, **excluding 2020–2021 pulls the estimate down to 30% (females) and 39% (males)** — but this is not a clean "no slowdown" reading either: it is pulled up by the genuine 2022–2024 recovery, which the original 2019-vintage analysis could not see. No single number is unambiguous; the pre-pandemic headline plus explicit out-of-sample validation (below) is the most honest framing. ## Out-of-sample validation The pre-pandemic (2011–2019) window is a forecast: it implies, for each population and sex, a best-supported mean annual $e_0$ gain equal to the 1991–2010 mean multiplied by the BF-maximising proportion. We can validate that forecast against what actually happened over 2020–2024 — years the pre-pandemic analysis could not use. ::: {#tbl-out-of-sample .cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Pre-2020-implied best mean annual gain (mu at the BF-maximising scenario) # versus what was actually observed over 2020-2024. pre2020_implied <- bf_argmax %>% filter(variant == "Pre-2020") %>% select(population, sex, implied_annual = mu_best) observed_2024 <- ch_e0_dta %>% filter(between(year, 2020, 2024)) %>% group_by(population, sex) %>% summarise( obs_2020 = ch_e0[year == 2020], obs_mean_2022_24 = mean(ch_e0[between(year, 2022, 2024)]), obs_mean_2020_24 = mean(ch_e0), .groups = "drop" ) validation_table <- pre2020_implied %>% left_join(observed_2024, by = c("population", "sex")) %>% mutate(population = factor(population, levels = populations)) %>% arrange(population, sex) validation_table %>% kable( digits = 3, col.names = c("Population", "Sex", "Pre-2020 implied annual gain", "Observed 2020", "Observed mean 2022-24", "Observed mean 2020-24"), caption = "Out-of-sample validation: pre-pandemic best-supported annual e0 gain (years) versus observed 2020-2024 changes. The 2024 actual is part-estimated (2024-based NPP base year)." ) %>% kable_styling() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

Population Sex Pre-2020 implied annual gain Observed 2020 Observed mean 2022-24 Observed mean 2020-24

United Kingdom male 0.121 -1.20 0.307 -0.020
England female 0.103 -0.93 0.257 0.012
England male 0.123 -1.25 0.320 -0.018
Scotland female 0.068 -0.51 0.267 0.020
Scotland male 0.112 -1.07 0.340 0.038
Wales female 0.046 -0.71 0.163 0.026
Wales male 0.084 -0.97 0.197 -0.074

Northern Ireland male 0.211 -0.81 0.033 -0.154
````` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} obs_series <- ch_e0_dta %>% filter(between(year, 2020, 2024)) %>% mutate(population = factor(population, levels = populations)) pre2020_implied %>% mutate(population = factor(population, levels = populations)) %>% ggplot() + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") + geom_hline(aes(yintercept = implied_annual), linetype = "dashed", colour = "steelblue") + geom_col(aes(x = year, y = ch_e0), data = obs_series, fill = "grey40", width = 0.7) + facet_grid(population ~ sex) + labs( x = "Year", y = "Annual change in e0 (years)", title = "Observed 2020-2024 annual e0 change vs pre-pandemic best forecast", subtitle = "Dashed line: mean annual gain implied by the 2011-2019 BF-maximising scenario", caption = "2024 actual is part-estimated (2024-based NPP base year)." ) ggsave(here("figures", "A14_out_of_sample_validation_2024.png"), height = 20, width = 25, units = "cm", dpi = 300) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](04_bayes_factors_files/figure-html/fig-out-of-sample-1.png){#fig-out-of-sample width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: The out-of-sample picture is dominated by two offsetting features. The **2020 shock** is far outside anything the pre-pandemic model contemplated (UK: −0.88 years female, −1.20 male). But the **2022–2024 recovery** is real and substantial: over 2022–2024 the UK averaged 0.247 years/year for females and 0.307 for males, both at or above the pre-pandemic best-supported gains of 0.098 (female) and 0.121 (male). Averaged across the whole 2020–2024 window the shock and recovery partly cancel (UK mean 0.010 female, -0.020 male). The substantive message is that the recovery materially weakens any naive "the stalling has only worsened" narrative: post-pandemic improvement has returned to roughly the reduced-but-positive rate the pre-2020 data already implied, rather than collapsing further. ## Summary * The corrected likelihood leaves every BF-maximising slowdown percentage unchanged relative to the buggy legacy version but restores meaningful magnitudes; these are reported here on the $\log_{10}$ scale. * The pre-pandemic headline (2011–2019) puts the UK slowdown at roughly 49% (females) / 56% (males), reproducing the original ~61% exactly for the 2011–2018 sub-window before the 2019 recovery year is added. * Extending to 2024 does not yield a single clean number: the full series is inflated by the 2020 shock (65% / 74%) and the COVID-excluded series is pulled up by the 2022–2024 recovery (30% / 39%). * Out-of-sample, the 2022–2024 recovery has returned improvement to about the rate the pre-2020 data implied — the single most important substantive update since the original analysis. ```
